title: Rhetorical technique Practice 2
description: 4 short texts - 8 focused rhetorical technique questions
subject: rla
passage:
TEXT A - Before and After

A photo essay shows the same vacant lot before cleanup and six months after it became a small community garden.

TEXT B - Training Analogy

The instructor compares a safety checklist to a pilot's preflight routine: both are meant to catch small problems before they become serious.

TEXT C - Bus Data

A proposal notes that 41 percent of surveyed late-shift workers reported missing the final bus at least once in the previous month.

TEXT D - Repair Urgency

"Fix the leak before the ceiling stains spread. Fix the wiring before another breaker fails. Fix the building while it is still repairable."

questions.prompt: Which rhetorical technique is most important in this example?
questions.explanation: Showing the same lot before cleanup and after it became a garden creates a direct visual comparison of change.
questions.rule: Name the relationship first, then prove it with the surrounding text.

options.text: visual before-and-after contrast
statistical evidence
options.whyWrong: No numerical measurement is described.

options.text: analogy
options.whyWrong: The photo essay does not compare the lot with a different familiar concept.

options.text: personal anecdote
options.whyWrong: The evidence is visual change at a place, not one person's story.

questions.prompt: What does the technique accomplish in this text?
questions.explanation: Using the same location at two times lets readers see the transformation rather than relying only on a verbal claim.
questions.rule: Name the relationship first, then prove it with the surrounding text.

options.text: It proves that every vacant lot will improve in the same way after six months.
options.whyWrong: One visual example cannot establish a universal outcome.

options.text: It explains the chronological steps volunteers used to build the garden.
options.whyWrong: The images show outcome contrast, not a process.

options.text: It makes the argument more emotional by quoting residents' reactions.
options.whyWrong: No quotations are part of the described technique.

options.text: The matched before-and-after views make the physical change easy to compare directly.

questions.prompt: Which rhetorical technique is most important in this example?
questions.explanation: Comparing the checklist with a pilot's preflight routine explains the value of repeated safety checks through a familiar parallel.
questions.rule: Name the relationship first, then prove it with the surrounding text.

options.text: statistic
options.whyWrong: No numerical evidence is used.

options.text: rhetorical question
options.whyWrong: No persuasive question is asked.

options.text: anecdote
options.whyWrong: The comparison is conceptual rather than a personal story.

options.text: analogy

questions.prompt: What does the technique accomplish in this text?
questions.explanation: The analogy transfers an understood safety principle from preflight checks to the training context.
questions.rule: Name the relationship first, then prove it with the surrounding text.

options.text: It proves the two jobs involve exactly the same risks and procedures.
options.whyWrong: An analogy highlights a useful similarity without making the situations identical.

options.text: It supplies numerical evidence that checklists reduce accidents.
options.whyWrong: The analogy explains a principle but gives no statistics.

options.text: The familiar comparison helps explain why repeating a checklist can be valuable even when the task feels routine.
It criticizes pilots for relying too heavily on routines.
options.whyWrong: The preflight routine is used positively to support repeated checks.

questions.prompt: Which rhetorical technique is most important in this example?
questions.explanation: The figure of 41 percent provides numerical evidence about how common the reported problem was in the surveyed group.
questions.rule: Name the relationship first, then prove it with the surrounding text.

options.text: anecdote
options.whyWrong: The sentence summarizes survey data rather than one worker's story.

options.text: analogy
options.whyWrong: No comparison to a separate familiar situation appears.

options.text: statistic
rhetorical question
options.whyWrong: The statement reports a measured percentage.

questions.prompt: What does the technique accomplish in this text?
questions.explanation: The statistic helps readers judge scale within the survey, while still being limited to the surveyed group and period.
questions.rule: Name the relationship first, then prove it with the surrounding text.

options.text: The percentage gives measurable evidence that missing the final bus affected a substantial share of the surveyed late-shift workers.
It proves that 41 percent of all workers in the city miss a bus every month.
options.whyWrong: The statistic applies to surveyed late-shift workers, not every worker in the city.

options.text: It explains why the final bus leaves at its current time.
options.whyWrong: The data measures reported missed service; it does not explain the schedule's cause.

options.text: It makes the proposal persuasive mainly by using emotionally charged vocabulary.
options.whyWrong: The technique is quantitative, not emotional.

questions.prompt: Which rhetorical technique is most important in this example?
questions.explanation: Repeating "Fix the... before..." creates a parallel series of commands that builds urgency.
questions.rule: Name the relationship first, then prove it with the surrounding text.

options.text: analogy
options.whyWrong: The lines do not compare repair work with another situation.

options.text: repetition and parallel imperative structure
statistic
options.whyWrong: No numerical evidence appears.

options.text: rhetorical question
options.whyWrong: The writer issues commands rather than questions.

questions.prompt: What does the technique accomplish in this text?
questions.explanation: Parallel repetition accumulates examples and makes delay sound increasingly risky.
questions.rule: Name the relationship first, then prove it with the surrounding text.

options.text: It proves that every listed problem will cause the building to fail immediately.
options.whyWrong: The wording urges prevention but does not establish inevitable immediate failure.

options.text: The repeated command builds urgency and links several maintenance problems into one call for action.
It presents three unrelated repairs with no common persuasive purpose.
options.whyWrong: The repeated structure deliberately connects the repairs.

options.text: It softens the recommendation by presenting repair as optional.
options.whyWrong: Imperative verbs strengthen rather than soften the call to act.
